title: A Grave in the Land of Promise
summary: Sarah dies at Hebron, and Abraham, a landless sojourner, buys the cave of Machpelah, his first legal foothold in the land God promised.
historicalContext: Some years after the binding of Isaac, the family is again near Hebron, the hill-country town where Abraham had pitched his tent by the oaks of Mamre and built an altar (13:18). Sarah is one hundred twenty-seven, so Isaac is about thirty-seven, and Abraham will live nearly four more decades. The local inhabitants are called “the sons of Heth,” a Canaanite people listed among the nations whose land God had pledged to Abraham’s seed (10:15; 15:20). Their names are Semitic and they converse with Abraham without an interpreter, so they belong to Canaan itself rather than to the distant Anatolian empire. In that world land normally passed by inheritance, and a resident alien had no ordinary right to own it. Transfers were made publicly at the city gate, before the men of standing who acted as witnesses, with silver weighed out on the scales, since coined money did not yet exist.
literaryContext: The chapter stands between the mountain of provision in Genesis 22 and the search for Isaac’s bride in Genesis 24. A short report of death and mourning (vv. 1–2) and a short report of burial (vv. 19–20) frame a long, carefully recorded negotiation in three rounds (vv. 3–6, 7–11, 12–16), followed by a formal description of the property deeded to Abraham (vv. 17–18). Key words carry the meaning: “bury” and “my dead” recur in nearly every speech, keeping grief at the center; “give” passes back and forth between buyer and seller; “hear” and “in the audience of” stress that the sale is witnessed; and “possession” ties the grave to God’s pledge of Canaan as “an everlasting possession” (17:8). God is never named in the chapter, yet the narrative shows faith acting through ordinary legal business. The cave purchased here becomes the family tomb of the patriarchs (25:9; 49:29–32; 50:13).
themes: Grief and faith held together at a graveside
Pilgrim identity among the people of the land
Integrity and courtesy in public dealings
A burial plot as a pledge of the promised inheritance
Death as sleep awaiting the resurrection

outline.title: Sarah’s Death and Abraham’s Mourning
outline.summary: Sarah dies at one hundred twenty-seven in Hebron, and Abraham comes to lament and weep for her.

outline.title: A Sojourner Asks for a Grave
outline.summary: Abraham confesses his alien status and requests a permanent burial possession; the Hittites honor him and offer their best tombs instead.

outline.title: The Request for Machpelah
outline.summary: Abraham names Ephron’s cave and offers full price, and Ephron publicly proposes to give him both the field and the cave.

outline.title: The Price Named and Paid
outline.summary: Abraham insists on paying, Ephron names four hundred shekels, and Abraham weighs out the silver at once before witnesses.

outline.title: The Deed and the Burial
outline.summary: The field, cave, and trees are confirmed to Abraham at the gate, and he lays Sarah to rest in the land of Canaan.

verses.bibleText: And Sarah was an hundred and seven and twenty years old: these were the years of the life of Sarah.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The chapter opens with a life measured by its full span: “Sarah was an hundred and seven and twenty years old.” No other woman in Scripture has her age at death recorded. The patriarchs receive such notices (25:7; 35:28; 47:28), and Sarah is placed alongside them. The Hebrew sentence is bracketed by the phrase “the life of Sarah,” at its beginning and again at its close, so that the verse reads like a memorial inscription honoring the woman through whom the promised line came.

The numbers carry their own story. Sarah bore Isaac at ninety (17:17), so her son is now about thirty-seven. Abraham, ten years older than she, is one hundred thirty-seven and will live another thirty-eight years (25:7). The three decades since Isaac’s birth are passed over in silence; the narrative moves directly from Moriah to this graveside. The woman who once laughed in disbelief behind the tent door (18:12) and later laughed for joy at the birth of her son (21:6) lived long enough to see the child of promise grow into a man.

Later Scripture remembers her as a woman of faith. Isaiah points the exiles to “Sarah that bare you” as evidence that God can multiply a family from a single couple (Isaiah 51:2). Hebrews says that she received strength to conceive because she judged God faithful (Hebrews 11:11), and Peter holds her up as a model of hope in God for believing women (1 Peter 3:5-6). The honest record of her failures in Egypt, with Hagar, and at Mamre is not erased; yet the final word on her is a life counted out in full years, every one of them under the care of the God who kept his word to her.

wordNotes.term: חַיֵּי שָׂרָה (ḥayyê Sarah) — the life of Sarah
wordNotes.explanation: Hebrew uses a plural form for “life,” and the phrase here stands at both ends of the verse, framing it. Later Jewish tradition named this section of Genesis after these words, an apt title since a chapter about a death begins by speaking twice of life. The same pattern, “these are the days of the years of the life of,” introduces Abraham’s own death notice (25:7), placing Sarah’s memorial on the same footing as the patriarch’s.

verses.bibleText: And Sarah died in Kirjath-arba; the same is Hebron in the land of Canaan: and Abraham came to mourn for Sarah, and to weep for her.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Sarah died.” The words are stated without detail of illness or last words. The place, however, is given with care: “in Kirjath-arba; the same is Hebron in the land of Canaan.” Kirjath-arba means “city of Arba” or “city of four,” and Joshua remembers Arba as a great man among the Anakim (Joshua 14:15). The narrator adds the later name, Hebron, so that Israelite readers would know the spot. The phrase “in the land of Canaan” is repeated at the burial (v. 19). Sarah does not die in Ur, Haran, or Egypt. She dies in the land God promised, and the whole chapter will turn on securing a place for her to rest there.

Abraham “came to mourn for Sarah, and to weep for her.” The verb may mean that he came into her tent, where mourners sat beside the body, or that he arrived from elsewhere; in either case he goes to where she lies. Two verbs describe his grief. The first refers to the formal lament, often loud, that marked a death in the ancient world; the second refers to tears. The man who had obeyed God’s hardest command without a recorded word of protest (22:3) now weeps openly. Scripture never treats such grief as faithlessness. Joseph wept over Jacob (50:1), and Jesus wept at the tomb of Lazarus moments before raising him (John 11:35).

Death was never part of God’s design. It entered with sin (Genesis 2:17; 3:19; Romans 5:12), and the patriarch’s tears acknowledge it as an enemy. Yet Scripture describes the death of God’s people as a sleep. Sarah does not go on to a conscious life somewhere else; she rests, unaware of the passing years, until the voice of the Son of God calls the dead from their graves (Daniel 12:2; John 5:28-29). Paul tells believers to sorrow, though not as those “which have no hope” (1 Thessalonians 4:13). Abraham’s tears and Abraham’s hope belong together, and the remainder of the chapter shows the hope taking concrete form.

wordNotes.term: לִסְפֹּד ... וְלִבְכֹּתָהּ (lispod ... welivkotah) — to mourn ... and to weep for her
wordNotes.explanation: The first verb describes public lament, the formal wailing and beating of the breast that accompanied death (1 Samuel 25:1; Zechariah 12:10). The second is the ordinary word for weeping. Together they express both the customary rite and the personal sorrow of a husband. In the Hebrew text the letter kaph in “to weep for her” is traditionally written small, a scribal feature later readers took as a sign of restrained grief, though the text itself simply records that Abraham wept.

verses.bibleText: And Abraham stood up from before his dead, and spake unto the sons of Heth, saying,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Abraham stood up from before his dead.” Mourners in the ancient Near East sat on the ground beside the corpse (Job 2:13; Lamentations 2:10). Rising marks the end of the first, private stage of grief and the beginning of action. Love for Sarah now takes the practical form of providing her a grave. The narrator does not report how long Abraham sat; he records that, when the time came, the patriarch got up and went to do what was needed.

The phrase “his dead” is striking. Sarah is not named again until her burial (v. 19). In the speeches that follow, “my dead” and “thy dead” recur again and again, nearly always near the close of a sentence. The repetition keeps the purpose of the negotiation constantly before the reader: a body lies waiting while men talk.

Abraham addresses “the sons of Heth,” descendants of Canaan’s son Heth (10:15). These local Hittites were one of the peoples whose land God had pledged to Abraham’s offspring (15:20). The irony is plain. The heir of the whole country must ask its present occupants for permission to bury his wife. God had told Abraham that his descendants would wait four generations before the land came into their hands (15:13-16). Until then, the promise would be held by faith, and Abraham conducts himself accordingly.

wordNotes.explanation: The participle “dead one” with a possessive suffix becomes a key word in the chapter, appearing in Abraham’s speeches and in the replies of the Hittites and Ephron (vv. 4, 6, 8, 11, 13, 15). It is a respectful way of referring to the deceased without repeating the name, and its frequency signals the urgency behind every polite exchange: burial in that climate could not be long delayed.

This verb, “to rise, stand,” opens the negotiation here and in verse 7, and the same form returns in verses 17 and 20, where the KJV renders it “were made sure.” Abraham rises to seek the land, and in the end the land “stands” legally confirmed to him, a wordplay that frames the transaction.

verses.bibleText: I am a stranger and a sojourner with you: give me a possession of a buryingplace with you, that I may bury my dead out of my sight.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Abraham begins with a confession of status: “I am a stranger and a sojourner with you.” The two words together describe a resident alien, someone who lives among a people with a recognized place but without the rights of a native landholder. Abraham had been in Canaan more than sixty years. He had defeated an invading coalition of kings (14:14-16) and made a treaty with the Philistine king Abimelech (21:22-32). He was wealthy and respected. Yet he makes no claim to rights he did not have, and he does not appeal to God’s promise as though it entitled him to seize land from its present owners. He presents his need humbly and asks for what only they could grant.

The request is specific: “give me a possession of a buryingplace.” A possession is property held permanently, passed down within a family. The word is used for Canaan itself in God’s covenant pledge, “all the land of Canaan, for an everlasting possession” (17:8). Abraham is not asking for a temporary favor. He wants a burial site that will belong to his household in perpetuity. That request explains the long negotiation that follows, for landowners in that world were reluctant to alienate family property, especially to an outsider.

His words became a lasting description of the people of faith. David prayed, “I am a stranger with thee, and a sojourner, as all my fathers were” (Psalm 39:12; compare 1 Chronicles 29:15). Hebrews says that the patriarchs “confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth,” and that by speaking so they showed they were seeking a better, heavenly country (Hebrews 11:13-16). Peter uses the same pair of Greek words found in the Greek Old Testament of this verse when he urges Christians to live as “strangers and pilgrims” who abstain from fleshly lusts (1 Peter 2:11).

That is the paradox of the verse. Abraham is a foreigner in the land, yet he asks to be buried in it. He will not return Sarah to Haran. By choosing a grave in Canaan he declares that his future, and his family’s, lies where God had pointed, even if the inheritance must wait beyond his own lifetime.

wordNotes.term: גֵּר־וְתוֹשָׁב (ger-wetoshav) — a stranger and a sojourner
wordNotes.explanation: A ger is a foreigner who has settled among another people; a toshav is a resident without inherited land. Joined, the words form a single idea, “resident alien.” The law of Moses later uses the same pair to describe Israel’s relation to God as the true owner of the land: “ye are strangers and sojourners with me” (Leviticus 25:23). The Greek Old Testament renders the phrase with the words Peter applies to believers in 1 Peter 2:11, so Abraham’s self-description becomes the church’s.

verses.bibleText: And the children of Heth answered Abraham, saying unto him,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And the children of Heth answered Abraham.” The verse is a simple speech formula, yet the narrator gives it a full line, as he does for each turn in the negotiation (vv. 3, 7, 10, 12-13, 14). The measured pace imitates the formal setting. This is a public conversation conducted by protocol, every exchange marked off and every party heard, much like the minutes of a legal proceeding.

The group answering is collective. Abraham has not yet named a particular owner, so the community as a whole responds. Land matters touched the entire town, since a sale to an outsider could alter inheritance, obligations, and boundaries. Only after the community has agreed in principle will a single landowner be brought into the discussion (v. 8). Abraham’s patience with this process is part of his integrity.

wordNotes.explanation: “Sons of Heth” identifies a people by their ancestor, Heth, the second son of Canaan (10:15). The narrator calls them by this name and also as “Hittites” (v. 10). Esau later married women from this people, to the grief of Isaac and Rebekah (26:34-35; 27:46), a contrast with Abraham’s careful distance from them in all but business.

verses.bibleText: Hear us, my lord: thou art a mighty prince among us: in the choice of our sepulchres bury thy dead; none of us shall withhold from thee his sepulchre, but that thou mayest bury thy dead.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The Hittites reply with high courtesy: “Hear us, my lord: thou art a mighty prince among us.” Abraham had placed himself at the bottom of their social order as a resident alien; they place him near the top. The title translated “mighty prince” is literally “prince of God.” Hebrew sometimes attaches the word for God to a noun to express the superlative, so the phrase can mean “a very great prince.” Even so, it recalls the earlier admission of Abimelech, “God is with thee in all that thou doest” (21:22). The people of the land recognize that the blessing of heaven rests on this landless man (12:2).

Their offer sounds generous: “in the choice of our sepulchres bury thy dead; none of us shall withhold from thee his sepulchre.” Family tombs in that region were usually caves or rock-cut chambers used for generations. To invite an outsider to lay his dead among one’s own family was a real honor. Yet there is a quiet shift in vocabulary. Abraham had asked for “a possession of a buryingplace” (v. 4), permanent property in his own name. They offer him the use of “our sepulchres.” They are willing to grant a grave but not land.

Abraham could have accepted. It would have been quicker, cheaper, and socially gracious. But burial in a Hittite family tomb would have blended his household into theirs, and the land would still have been someone else’s. His request had a purpose beyond Sarah’s immediate need. He wanted a foothold in the land of promise that belonged to his line, and he would not exchange that for an honorable but borrowed resting place. Faith sometimes declines a kind offer because it aims at something the giver does not yet understand.

wordNotes.term: נְשִׂיא אֱלֹהִים (nesiʾ ʾelohim) — a mighty prince
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “prince of God.” A nasiʾ is a chief or leader, the term later used for the heads of Israel’s tribes (Numbers 7:2). Adding ʾelohim can intensify a phrase, as with the “mountains of God,” rendered “great mountains” (Psalm 36:6). The KJV’s “mighty prince” captures that sense, though the wording also hints that his standing comes from God.

verses.bibleText: And Abraham stood up, and bowed himself to the people of the land, even to the children of Heth.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Abraham stood up, and bowed himself to the people of the land.” The man just called a prince of God bows to the townspeople. He does not argue with their offer or correct their wording. He thanks them, honoring their courtesy with his own, and then moves the discussion forward. The bow is the customary gesture of respect and gratitude, the same act Abraham performed when the three visitors arrived at Mamre (18:2).

“The people of the land” here seems to mean the citizens with standing in the community, the landholding men whose consent was needed for any transfer of property, rather than the whole population. A similar body of elders sat at the gate of Bethlehem when Boaz redeemed Naomi’s field (Ruth 4:9-11). Abraham addresses them as the proper authority.

His conduct is a lesson in how the people of God may live among neighbors who do not share their faith. He is respectful without compromise, grateful without becoming dependent, and humble without losing his purpose. Paul’s counsel, “If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men” (Romans 12:18), finds an early illustration at Hebron. Abraham’s faith shows itself in good manners as well as in altars.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb describes bending low or prostrating oneself, an act of homage. It is used for worship of God (22:5, where Abraham says he and the lad will go “worship”), and also for courtesy toward people of rank (33:3; 42:6). Context decides the sense. Here it is social deference and thanks, repeated at the next stage of the negotiation (v. 12).

wordNotes.term: עַם־הָאָרֶץ (ʿam-haʾarets) — the people of the land
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase can refer to a general population, but in many Old Testament contexts it denotes the enfranchised citizens who held land and took part in public decisions (2 Kings 11:14; 21:24). That fits here, where these men act as the body before whom property changes hands.

verses.bibleText: And he communed with them, saying, If it be your mind that I should bury my dead out of my sight; hear me, and intreat for me to Ephron the son of Zohar,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Having received general permission, Abraham turns to specifics: “If it be your mind that I should bury my dead out of my sight; hear me, and intreat for me to Ephron the son of Zohar.” The conditional opening restates their own words back to them. If they truly mean that he may bury his dead among them, then let them help him obtain the particular place he has in mind.

Abraham does not approach Ephron directly. He asks the assembly to speak on his behalf. That was a sensible way to proceed in a community where land deals were public matters. With the town’s leaders acting as go-betweens, the owner would be under social pressure to deal fairly, and the buyer would be protected against later charges of having taken advantage. It also allowed Ephron to save face; he would be responding to his peers as well as to a foreigner.

Ephron is identified as “the son of Zohar.” Non-Israelites in Genesis are seldom named with their fathers (compare 34:2), and the detail suggests a family of some prominence. Abraham evidently knew the property and its owner well. He had lived in this area for years before moving to the Negev (13:18; 20:1), and he arrives at the negotiation with a precise request already formed.

The repeated phrase “bury my dead out of my sight” is honest and unsentimental. A body decays; love requires that it be laid to rest. Abraham does not pretend otherwise. His grief is real, and so is his practical attention to what must be done.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb pagaʿ means “to meet” or “encounter,” and with certain prepositions it means to approach someone with a request on another’s behalf, to intercede. God tells Jeremiah not to “make intercession” for the people using this verb (Jeremiah 7:16), and Ruth uses it when she asks Naomi not to “intreat” her to leave (Ruth 1:16). Abraham asks the assembly to press his case with Ephron.

verses.bibleText: That he may give me the cave of Machpelah, which he hath, which is in the end of his field; for as much money as it is worth he shall give it me for a possession of a buryingplace amongst you.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Abraham names the place: “the cave of Machpelah, which he hath, which is in the end of his field.” Machpelah appears in Scripture only in connection with this cave and its field (25:9; 49:30; 50:13). The name is related to a Hebrew word meaning “double,” and the Greek Old Testament translates it “the double cave.” It may describe a cave with two chambers. Over the centuries the site came to be identified with the cave beneath the great enclosure in Hebron that tradition associates with the patriarchs, though the lower chambers have never been open to careful study.

Two details in the request are calculated. The cave lies “in the end of his field,” at its edge. Selling it would not divide or impair the use of the rest of Ephron’s land. Abraham is making it easy for the owner to agree. And he offers to pay “as much money as it is worth,” literally “for full silver.” This is the language of a cash sale, complete and final. Abraham is not asking for a gift or a favor. He intends to pay the whole price so that no one can later claim the land was only lent or that the transaction was incomplete.

The phrase “for a possession of a buryingplace” returns from verse 4. Abraham has not been distracted by the offer of a Hittite family tomb. He wants a place that is legally his. That determination will cost him, and he knows it. A man who had received a ram on Moriah in place of his son (22:13) had learned that God’s provision is real. Here he does what lies in his own hands: he pays fully and honestly, trusting God for the rest of the inheritance he would not live to see.

Abraham’s offer also guards God’s honor. Earlier he refused to take so much as a sandal thong from the king of Sodom, “lest thou shouldest say, I have made Abram rich” (14:23). He would owe his position in Canaan to God and to fair dealing, not to the generosity of its inhabitants.

wordNotes.explanation: The name always carries the definite article in Hebrew, “the Machpelah,” suggesting a descriptive name for the site. It is related to the verb kafal, “to double” (Exodus 26:9), and the Greek Old Testament renders it “the double cave.” Whatever its shape, the name became attached to the family tomb in which Sarah, Abraham, Isaac, Rebekah, Leah, and Jacob were laid.

wordNotes.term: בְּכֶסֶף מָלֵא (bekesef maleʾ) — for as much money as it is worth
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “for full silver.” The expression denotes payment of the entire price, a sale made final rather than a loan or partial transfer. David uses the same phrase when he insists on buying Ornan’s threshing floor “for the full price” (1 Chronicles 21:22, 24).

verses.bibleText: And Ephron dwelt among the children of Heth: and Ephron the Hittite answered Abraham in the audience of the children of Heth, even of all that went in at the gate of his city, saying,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Ephron dwelt among the children of Heth.” The Hebrew can mean that Ephron was sitting among them at that moment. He is present in the assembly, and the request intended for him through intermediaries reaches him directly. He does not wait for others to speak on Abraham’s behalf; he answers for himself. His willingness to respond in his own person means that whatever follows will be his free decision.

The narrator lingers on the audience: Ephron answered “in the audience of the children of Heth, even of all that went in at the gate of his city.” The city gate was the place of public business in the ancient world. Elders sat there to hear disputes and witness contracts (Deuteronomy 21:19; Ruth 4:1-11; Proverbs 31:23). The phrase “all that went in at the gate” likely refers to the men who had full rights in the town’s affairs. The entire legally competent community is listening.

That publicity is the point. In a society where many agreements were oral, witnesses served as the record. The sale of Machpelah would not depend on one man’s memory or goodwill. Generations later, Jacob could point to this field and say exactly where it was and who had bought it (49:29-32), because it had been settled at the gate before everyone who mattered.

wordNotes.explanation: Literally “in the ears of.” The idiom appears repeatedly in this chapter (vv. 13, 16) and stresses that words were spoken in the hearing of witnesses. In an oral legal culture, being heard by the proper people made an agreement binding. Moses uses the same idiom when he speaks the song of witness “in the ears of all the congregation” (Deuteronomy 31:30).

verses.bibleText: Nay, my lord, hear me: the field give I thee, and the cave that is therein, I give it thee; in the presence of the sons of my people give I it thee: bury thy dead.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Ephron’s reply is lavish: “Nay, my lord, hear me: the field give I thee, and the cave that is therein, I give it thee; in the presence of the sons of my people give I it thee: bury thy dead.” Three times in one sentence he says “I give.” Abraham asked only for the cave; Ephron offers the whole field, and offers it free.

How should the offer be read? In the courtesy of the ancient Near East, an opening proposal to give something as a gift often served as a polite prelude to naming a price. Both parties understood the form. Abraham’s response (v. 13) shows that he did not take the gift at face value, and Ephron’s quick mention of four hundred shekels (v. 15) confirms that payment was expected. The offer was courteous, but it was not a real gift.

There may also have been a practical reason for including the field. Ancient law codes from the Hittite heartland linked certain obligations to landowners and allowed them to be transferred only when an entire property changed hands. Whether or not such rules applied at Hebron, Ephron shows no interest in parting with the cave alone. He wants to sell all of it.

A gift, moreover, would not have served Abraham’s purpose. What one man gives, his heirs might later dispute or reclaim. Accepting would have left Abraham’s family on the land by permission. A purchase at full price before witnesses would make it theirs by right. Abraham’s faith looked further ahead than the burial at hand. He was securing for his descendants a place that no one could later contest.

wordNotes.explanation: The Hebrew uses the perfect tense, literally “I have given,” a form commonly used for a declaration that takes effect as it is spoken, as in legal or covenant settings (15:18, “unto thy seed have I given this land”). Ephron uses this formal language three times, while the verb “give” runs through the whole negotiation, passing back and forth between seller and buyer.

verses.bibleText: And Abraham bowed down himself before the people of the land.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Abraham bowed down himself before the people of the land.” For the second time he bows (v. 7). The gesture acknowledges Ephron’s generous words and the assembly’s goodwill. It also gives Abraham a moment to frame his answer carefully. He will decline the gift without giving offense.

Notice the audience again. Abraham bows before “the people of the land,” not only before Ephron. He addresses the whole body of witnesses because the next words he speaks must be heard by them all. The courtesy is public, and so is the transaction it prepares.

Abraham’s repeated bowing shows that humility and resolve can live together. He yields on every point of etiquette and on none of substance. That combination is rare and valuable among believers who must deal with the world’s institutions. Peter’s counsel to “honour all men” (1 Peter 2:17) fits the patriarch at the gate, who honored his neighbors while keeping his eyes fixed on God’s promise.

wordNotes.explanation: Literally “to the face of,” the preposition places Abraham in the presence of the assembled citizens. The narrator varies it with “in the audience of” (v. 13) and “in the presence of” (v. 18), all of which stress that every step happened in full view of those who could later testify to it.

verses.bibleText: And he spake unto Ephron in the audience of the people of the land, saying, But if thou wilt give it, I pray thee, hear me: I will give thee money for the field; take it of me, and I will bury my dead there.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Abraham speaks to Ephron, but “in the audience of the people of the land”: “But if thou wilt give it, I pray thee, hear me: I will give thee money for the field; take it of me, and I will bury my dead there.” The Hebrew is halting and emphatic, almost as if Abraham interrupts himself: “If only you would hear me!” The patriarch is earnest. He wants this settled, and he wants it settled properly.

He accepts Ephron’s terms on the extent of the property. He had asked for the cave; now he agrees to buy “the field.” But he turns Ephron’s language of giving into the language of payment. “I will give thee money” uses the same verb Ephron used three times, now reversed: what Ephron offered to give, Abraham will pay for. “Take it of me” presses the point. Abraham refuses to be indebted.

The principle is the same one David later voiced when Araunah offered him the threshing floor for nothing: “neither will I offer burnt offerings unto the LORD my God of that which doth cost me nothing” (2 Samuel 24:24). Abraham will not lay the foundation of his family’s inheritance on someone else’s generosity. He pays, and his claim will be beyond question.

His closing words return to the purpose that has driven the whole conversation: “and I will bury my dead there.” Everything else is preliminary. Abraham wants Sarah laid to rest in ground that belongs to the family of promise.

wordNotes.term: לוּ שְׁמָעֵנִי (lu shemaʿeni) — I pray thee, hear me
wordNotes.explanation: The particle lu expresses an earnest wish, “O that” or “if only” (17:18, “O that Ishmael might live before thee”). Combined with the plea “hear me,” it gives Abraham’s words a tone of urgency beneath the courtesy, as he pushes past the offered gift toward a proper sale.

verses.bibleText: And Ephron answered Abraham, saying unto him,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Ephron answered Abraham, saying unto him.” Once more the narrator gives a speech introduction its own verse. The repetition slows the scene to the pace of the negotiation itself, each turn deliberate and witnessed.

This time Ephron answers Abraham alone, “saying unto him.” The earlier rounds involved the whole assembly. Now the conversation has narrowed to buyer and seller, and the next sentence will name the price. Readers are made to wait for it, as Abraham did.

wordNotes.explanation: The ordinary verb for replying, used here as in verses 5 and 10 to mark each turn of the dialogue. Its steady recurrence gives the chapter the shape of a recorded proceeding in which every party’s words are formally noted.

verses.bibleText: My lord, hearken unto me: the land is worth four hundred shekels of silver; what is that betwixt me and thee? bury therefore thy dead.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
At last Ephron names his figure: “My lord, hearken unto me: the land is worth four hundred shekels of silver; what is that betwixt me and thee? bury therefore thy dead.” The price is wrapped in the same courtesy as the earlier offer of a gift. Between friends and men of means, he implies, such a sum hardly deserves mention.

The amount was large. A shekel was a unit of weight, roughly eleven or twelve grams, so four hundred shekels came to well over four kilograms of silver. Scripture supplies some comparisons. Joseph was sold for twenty pieces of silver (37:28). Jeremiah later bought a family field at Anathoth for seventeen shekels (Jeremiah 32:9). David paid fifty shekels for Araunah’s threshing floor and oxen (2 Samuel 24:24). Prices varied by time, place, and the size of the plot, and the dimensions of Ephron’s field are unknown. Even so, the figure appears steep, and Ephron seems to have recognized that a grieving man of wealth was in no position to bargain long.

Ephron’s phrase “what is that betwixt me and thee?” is a polite invitation to accept without fuss. It may also have been an opening bid, leaving room for haggling, as was customary in the marketplace. Abraham does not take up the opening. To bargain over Sarah’s grave would have been unseemly, and to beat down the price would have given Ephron or his heirs grounds for later complaint.

The final words, “bury therefore thy dead,” are the last of many references in the speeches to the dead awaiting burial. The negotiation has run its course. All that remains is for Abraham to decide whether the price is worth paying. He has already made up his mind. The promise of God is worth more to him than silver.

wordNotes.term: אַרְבַּע מֵאֹת שֶׁקֶל־כֶּסֶף (ʾarbaʿ meʾot sheqel-kesef) — four hundred shekels of silver
wordNotes.explanation: The shekel was a measure of weight before it became a coin; the noun comes from the verb shaqal, “to weigh,” used in verse 16. Silver was the common medium of exchange in the patriarchal period. Four hundred shekels equaled several kilograms of metal, a sum that only a wealthy man such as Abraham (13:2; 24:35) could pay at once.

A rhetorical question meant to minimize the sum, “what is it?” The courteous understatement lets Ephron name a high price without appearing grasping, while placing the burden of politeness on the buyer to accept graciously.

verses.bibleText: And Abraham hearkened unto Ephron; and Abraham weighed to Ephron the silver, which he had named in the audience of the sons of Heth, four hundred shekels of silver, current money with the merchant.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Abraham hearkened unto Ephron.” Abraham neither haggles nor delays. He “weighed to Ephron the silver, which he had named in the audience of the sons of Heth, four hundred shekels of silver, current money with the merchant.” The deal is concluded on the spot.

The verb “weighed” reflects the economy of the day. There were no coins yet; payment meant placing pieces or rings of silver on a balance against standard weights. Each step happens before witnesses. The amount Abraham pays is exactly the amount Ephron named “in the audience of the sons of Heth.” No one can later say the figure was disputed, short, or different from what was agreed. The narrator repeats the sum, “four hundred shekels of silver,” as a contract would.

“Current money with the merchant” means silver measured by the standard accepted among traders. Weights could be manipulated, and Scripture later condemns those who keep “divers weights” to cheat customers (Deuteronomy 25:13-16; Proverbs 11:1). Abraham pays by the recognized commercial standard, so the quality and quantity of the payment can be checked by anyone familiar with trade. He leaves no room for suspicion.

Centuries later, as Babylon besieged Jerusalem, Jeremiah bought a field at Anathoth. He too weighed the silver on the scales, signed the deed, called witnesses, and stored the documents so they would last (Jeremiah 32:9-15). That purchase was a public declaration that God would restore Israel to its land. Abraham’s payment at Hebron carries the same meaning. A man who owned nothing in Canaan spent a large sum on a grave because he believed that God would one day give his descendants the whole land.

The silver Abraham weighed out was a confession of faith. It declared before the Hittites, more plainly than words could, that the promise was real enough to invest in.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb shaqal means to weigh out on a balance, the normal way of paying before coinage (Ezra 8:25-26; Jeremiah 32:9-10). Payment was only as honest as the scales and weights used, which is why the law and the prophets insist on true measures (Leviticus 19:36; Amos 8:5).

wordNotes.term: עֹבֵר לַסֹּחֵר (ʿover lassoḥer) — current money with the merchant
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “passing over to the trader,” meaning silver that would be accepted in commerce, of standard weight and quality. The soḥer was a traveling trader (37:28 uses a related form for the Midianite merchants), so the phrase points to a recognized commercial standard rather than a private or local reckoning.

verses.bibleText: And the field of Ephron, which was in Machpelah, which was before Mamre, the field, and the cave which was therein, and all the trees that were in the field, that were in all the borders round about, were made sure

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The narrator now records the deed: “the field of Ephron, which was in Machpelah, which was before Mamre, the field, and the cave which was therein, and all the trees that were in the field, that were in all the borders round about, were made sure.” The sentence piles up specific items as a legal document would, describing the property and its contents so that nothing could later be disputed. The thought runs on into verse 18 without a break.

“Before Mamre” means east of Mamre. A Hebrew speaker giving directions faced east, so “before” could indicate that direction. Mamre was the grove where Abraham had lived and built an altar (13:18; 18:1), the place where he had received the promise of Isaac. The grave lies within sight of the old home.

The inclusion of “all the trees” is a telling detail. Contracts of land sale from the ancient Near East commonly listed trees, and sometimes counted them, because trees had economic value in fruit and timber. Without that clause the seller or his heirs might claim the produce. Abraham’s title included everything on the land, and the borders were fixed “round about.”

The verb “were made sure” is the same verb that described Abraham’s rising in verses 3 and 7. He stood up to seek a possession; now the possession stands, confirmed and legally valid. What began in grief ends in a secure title. God had told Abraham to walk through the land “in the length of it and in the breadth of it” (13:17). For the first time a piece of it, with defined boundaries, is his.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb qum, “to rise, stand,” in a legal sense means to be established or confirmed, as a vow that “shall stand” (Numbers 30:4) or a matter established by witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15). Here it states that the transfer of the field is valid and binding.

The Hebrew noun is singular, used collectively for the trees of the field. Their inclusion in the description reflects careful conveyancing practice; trees were valuable property, and the law later protected fruit trees even in time of war (Deuteronomy 20:19).

verses.bibleText: Unto Abraham for a possession in the presence of the children of Heth, before all that went in at the gate of his city.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The sentence concludes: the property was made sure “unto Abraham for a possession in the presence of the children of Heth, before all that went in at the gate of his city.” The witness clause echoes verse 10 almost word for word. The same assembly that heard Ephron’s offer now witnesses the transfer. No secret dealing or private arrangement is involved. The whole town knows that this field belongs to Abraham.

That public character matters for the rest of Genesis. When Jacob, dying in Egypt, instructs his sons to bury him at Machpelah, he describes the field precisely and recalls that Abraham bought it from Ephron the Hittite (49:29-32; 50:13). The family’s claim rested on a transaction everyone in Hebron had seen.

Faith in this chapter does not bypass the ordinary structures of law and community. Abraham works through them with care, so that the possession God would ultimately give his family begins with a title no one could fairly challenge.

wordNotes.explanation: This noun differs from the word for “possession” in verses 4, 9, and 20. Miqnah means something acquired by purchase. It describes servants “bought with money” (17:12-13), and Jeremiah’s deed is called “the evidence of the purchase” (Jeremiah 32:11). The term stresses how Abraham acquired the land: he bought it.

verses.bibleText: And after this, Abraham buried Sarah his wife in the cave of the field of Machpelah before Mamre: the same is Hebron in the land of Canaan.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And after this, Abraham buried Sarah his wife in the cave of the field of Machpelah before Mamre: the same is Hebron in the land of Canaan.” After many verses of negotiation, the burial itself is told in a single sentence. Sarah is called by name again for the first time since verse 2, and now with the tender addition “his wife.” Throughout the bargaining she has been “my dead”; at the grave she is Sarah, Abraham’s wife of many decades.

The narrator repeats the location in full: Machpelah, before Mamre, Hebron, “in the land of Canaan.” The final phrase links the burial to the opening notice of her death (v. 2) and, beyond that, to God’s promise. Sarah had left Ur and Haran with her husband to go to a land she had not seen (12:5). She died in that land, and now she is laid to rest in a part of it that belongs to her family. Hebrews says of the patriarchs and their households, “These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off” (Hebrews 11:13). Sarah’s grave is a sign that the promise was still in force.

The chapter does not say that Sarah went anywhere at death. Scripture’s consistent picture is that the dead rest in the grave, without awareness, until the resurrection. She is not conscious in some other realm; she sleeps. Job looked forward to seeing God “in my flesh” after his body had decayed (Job 19:25-27). Daniel was told that “many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake” (Daniel 12:2). Jesus called the death of Lazarus a sleep and then woke him (John 11:11-14, 43-44). Paul teaches that “the dead in Christ shall rise first” when the Lord descends from heaven with the trumpet of God (1 Thessalonians 4:16). Sarah awaits that day. Her hope, like Abraham’s, lies in the God who raises the dead (Hebrews 11:19).

The scene also anticipates another burial. Abraham, the heir of a whole land, had to buy a grave from strangers. Jesus, the true Seed of Abraham and heir of all things, was laid in a borrowed tomb provided by Joseph of Arimathea (Matthew 27:57-60). His grave was empty on the third day, and his resurrection is the firstfruits of the harvest that will include Sarah and all who sleep in faith (1 Corinthians 15:20-23). The cave at Machpelah held its dead in hope; the garden tomb near Jerusalem guarantees that the hope will be fulfilled.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb “to bury” is the dominant word of the chapter, and with its related noun for “grave” or “sepulchre” it appears over a dozen times. Here the long-anticipated action finally takes place. Burial in Scripture is the respectful return of the body to the ground from which it came (3:19), carried out in expectation of the day when “they that are in the graves shall hear his voice” (John 5:28-29).

A simple marker of sequence: the burial follows the completed sale. The ordering shows Abraham’s priority. He did not lay Sarah in a temporary or borrowed place while the details were sorted out; he buried her once the ground was legally his family’s (compare 25:9-10).

verses.bibleText: And the field, and the cave that is therein, were made sure unto Abraham for a possession of a buryingplace by the sons of Heth.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The chapter closes with a summary: “the field, and the cave that is therein, were made sure unto Abraham for a possession of a buryingplace by the sons of Heth.” The phrase “a possession of a buryingplace” is exactly what Abraham asked for at the beginning (v. 4). His request has been granted in full, by the very people who first offered him something less.

Stephen, recounting Israel’s history before the council, observed that God gave Abraham “none inheritance in it, no, not so much as to set his foot on,” even while promising the land to him and his seed (Acts 7:5). That is the striking point of Genesis 23. After decades in Canaan, the only ground Abraham ever owned there was a grave, and he had to pay for it. The promise was sure, but its fulfillment lay beyond his lifetime.

Yet the field at Machpelah was far from meaningless. It was a pledge, a first portion held in hand, testifying that the rest would follow. Isaac and Rebekah, Jacob and Leah would be buried there (49:31; 50:13). When Israel came out of Egypt centuries later, they were returning to a land where their ancestors already lay. The patriarchs owned Canaan in death before their children possessed it in life.

The New Testament carries the promise further. Abraham was to be “the heir of the world” (Romans 4:13), and he looked for “a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God” (Hebrews 11:10). Jesus promised that the meek would inherit the earth (Matthew 5:5), and the Bible closes with a new heaven and a new earth where God dwells with his people (Revelation 21:1-3). That inheritance will be received when the dead in Christ are raised at his coming. Abraham and Sarah will receive it together with all the faithful, “that they without us should not be made perfect” (Hebrews 11:39-40).

wordNotes.term: אֲחֻזַּת־קָבֶר (ʾaḥuzzat-qaver) — a possession of a buryingplace
wordNotes.explanation: ʾAḥuzzah denotes landed property held permanently and passed down within a family. The word frames the chapter (vv. 4, 9, 20) and links the grave to God’s covenant pledge of Canaan as “an everlasting possession” (17:8; 48:4). The law later regulated the redemption of such family holdings so that they would not be lost permanently (Leviticus 25:24-25). Abraham’s burial plot was the first ʾaḥuzzah in Canaan held by the family of promise.

teachingNotes.openingQuestion: What does the way a person buries the dead reveal about what that person expects God to do?
teachingNotes.mainPoint: Abraham meets Sarah’s death with honest grief and careful integrity, and by securing a grave in Canaan he declares his confidence that God’s promise outlasts death.
discussionQuestions: Why does the narrator spend two verses on Sarah’s death and fourteen on the purchase of a grave?
Why might Abraham have refused the Hittites’ offer of their finest tombs and Ephron’s offer of a free gift?
How does Abraham’s conduct at the gate model integrity for believers who live among people of other convictions?
What does Hebrews 11:13-16 add to our understanding of this chapter?
How does the hope of the resurrection shape Christian grief at a graveside?
commonMisunderstandings: Abraham’s weeping does not show weak faith; Scripture treats mourning as a fitting response to death.
The grave at Machpelah was not the fulfillment of the land promise; it was a small pledge that pointed beyond Abraham’s lifetime.
Sarah did not pass at death into conscious existence elsewhere; she was laid to rest to sleep until the resurrection.
teachingNotes.emphasis: Keep together the reality of death, the honesty of grief, and the firmness of the promise: Abraham buries Sarah as one who expects God to keep his word on the far side of the grave.
teachingNotes.closingAppeal: Live as a pilgrim who deals honestly with neighbors, grieve with hope, and anchor your expectations in the God who raises the dead.

evangelisticNotes.mainDoctrinalTheme: Death is a real enemy and a sleep from which God will awaken his people at Christ’s return, when the promised inheritance is fully given.
flow: Even the woman of promise died; death reaches every life because of sin.
Abraham grieved openly, yet he buried Sarah in the land God had promised, not back in Mesopotamia.
Scripture calls the death of believers a sleep, without awareness, until the resurrection morning.
Christ, who lay in a borrowed tomb and rose, guarantees that the sleeping saints will be raised at his coming.
All who trust him may face death as pilgrims with a sure inheritance ahead.
simpleIllustrations: A small down payment on a house says that the buyer expects the rest of the contract to be honored; the cave was Abraham’s down payment on Canaan.
A parent who tucks a child into bed says “good night,” not “good-bye,” because morning is coming.
evangelisticNotes.appealQuestion: Will you place your hope in the Lord who promises to awaken those who sleep in him and give them the inheritance?
cautions: Do not rush grieving people past their sorrow; Abraham wept before he negotiated.
Do not describe the dead as already enjoying conscious reward; keep to Scripture’s language of sleep and resurrection.
Do not turn the chapter into a lesson on real estate shrewdness; its focus is faith in the promise.

reflectionQuestions: When I lose someone I love, do I allow myself to grieve while still holding to God’s promises?
Where do I live as a settled resident of this world rather than as a pilgrim on the way to God’s inheritance?
How would my neighbors describe my honesty in money matters and public dealings?
What small, concrete step of faith could I take today that only makes sense if God’s promises are true?
How does the hope of the resurrection change the way I think about my own death?
